title: IP addressing and special ranges
intro: Knowledge-based questions on IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose address ranges. Write addresses in canonical notation (e.g. `10.0.0.0/8`, `::1`). These ranges appear constantly in packet captures and firewall logs.

questions.prompt: What is the IPv4 loopback address?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **127.0.0.1** is the standard loopback address (the entire 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved). Traffic sent here never leaves the host's network stack.

questions.prompt: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **::1** is the IPv6 loopback ([RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291)). Equivalent to 127.0.0.1. Services binding only to `::1` are not reachable from other hosts.

questions.prompt: What RFC 1918 private address range uses a /8 prefix?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **10.0.0.0/8** — 16,777,216 addresses. Commonly used in large enterprise and data-centre networks. The three [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918) ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are non-routable on the public internet.

questions.prompt: What RFC 1918 private address range uses a /12 prefix?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **172.16.0.0/12** covers 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 (1,048,576 addresses). Often used for cloud VPC default ranges (AWS uses 172.31.0.0/16 by default).

questions.prompt: What IPv4 range is automatically assigned when DHCP fails (link-local / APIPA)?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **169.254.0.0/16** ([RFC 3927](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3927), APIPA). A host assigns itself an address in this range when it cannot reach a DHCP server. Seeing 169.254.x.x in logs or `ip addr` output indicates a DHCP failure.

questions.prompt: What IPv6 prefix is used for link-local addresses?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **fe80::/10** ([RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291)). Every IPv6 interface automatically configures a link-local address derived from its MAC (EUI-64) or via privacy extensions. Link-local addresses are only valid on a single link and are never routed.

questions.prompt: What CIDR block does RFC 6598 reserve for Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT)?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **100.64.0.0/10** ([RFC 6598](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598)) — the shared address space for CGNAT. ISPs use this between their CPE and CGNAT devices. If you see 100.64–100.127 addresses in captures, you are behind a CGNAT and your public IP is shared with other subscribers.

questions.prompt: What is the IPv4 limited broadcast address?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **255.255.255.255** — delivered to all hosts on the local network segment. Routers do not forward it. DHCP Discover and BOOTP use this as the destination before the client has an address.

questions.prompt: What IPv4 CIDR range is reserved for multicast groups?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **224.0.0.0/4** ([RFC 5771](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5771)) covers 224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255. Notable sub-ranges: 224.0.0.0/24 (link-local multicast, e.g. OSPF hello on 224.0.0.5), 239.0.0.0/8 (administratively scoped).

questions.prompt: What IPv6 prefix identifies Unique Local Addresses (ULA), the IPv6 equivalent of RFC 1918 private ranges?
questions.solutionMarkdown: **fc00::/7** ([RFC 4193](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4193)) — covers fc00:: through fdff::. The `fd` prefix (fdxx::/48 per site) is locally assigned; `fc` is reserved for future central assignment. ULAs are not routed on the public internet.

summaryMarkdown:
## Purpose

Instant recognition of these ranges prevents misreading logs and captures. A 10.x source in an internet-facing capture means NAT is involved. A 169.254.x source means a configuration failure. A fe80:: source is always link-local.

## Quick-reference table

| Range | RFC | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 10.0.0.0/8 | [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918) | Private |
| 100.64.0.0/10 | [RFC 6598](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598) | CGNAT shared |
| 127.0.0.0/8 | — | Loopback |
| 169.254.0.0/16 | [RFC 3927](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3927) | Link-local / APIPA |
| 172.16.0.0/12 | [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918) | Private |
| 192.0.2.0/24 | [RFC 5737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737) | Documentation (TEST-NET-1) |
| 192.168.0.0/16 | [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918) | Private |
| 198.51.100.0/24 | [RFC 5737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737) | Documentation (TEST-NET-2) |
| 203.0.113.0/24 | [RFC 5737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737) | Documentation (TEST-NET-3) |
| 224.0.0.0/4 | [RFC 5771](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5771) | Multicast |
| 240.0.0.0/4 | — | Reserved |
| 255.255.255.255 | — | Limited broadcast |
| ::1/128 | [RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291) | IPv6 loopback |
| fc00::/7 | [RFC 4193](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4193) | IPv6 ULA (private) |
| fe80::/10 | [RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291) | IPv6 link-local |
